results.verified_title: Governing the de-risking agenda: policy instrument mixes in Scandinavian research collaboration with China
results.source_identity_basis: The 28 March 2026 Education Inquiry paper by Hans Lundin and Tommy Shih matches the DOI, title, publisher and research-portal record. Substantive abstract, Methods §4, Results §5 and Conclusion §7 are indexed from the publisher; ordinary publisher page fetch was blocked (403). The same document is separately assigned to Norway.
results.evidence_location: Abstract; §4 Method; §§5.1–5.3 country-specific results; §§6–7 discussion and conclusions.
results.specific_finding: The paper documents how Denmark, Norway and Sweden govern research collaboration WITH China, rather than a change in China’s own R&I funding, institutions or talent system.
results.primary_evidence_summary: Comparative documentary and interview-based assessment distinguishes Denmark’s reinforced security-oriented mix, Norway’s layered negotiated configuration and Sweden’s less coordinated configuration; author explicitly disclaims causal effect estimation.
results.corroboration_assessment: University repository independently identifies the paper; Norwegian government interviews support Norway’s institutional concerns, not a domestic Chinese policy finding. No independent China-side institutional mechanism was demonstrated by this assigned work.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: Important for EU and non-EU European research-security governance, but cannot be counted as an independent Chinese domestic R&I development solely because China is a cooperation partner.
results.eu_radar_comparison: The main Radar exactly includes this paper. Change its country interpretation: Scandinavian institutional response, not evidence of structural change inside China. Retain the independently valid Norway-specific assessment under candidate 3fa1388ff31d867abb0d489c.
results.method_and_limitations: Limited three-country qualitative comparative design; explicitly noncausal; no reconstruction of Chinese institutions/policies; publisher direct web fetching blocked but indexed substantive source and university record were checked.
results.reason_for_review_or_drop: Country attribution fails the assigned China domestic research-institutions question. Duplicate document_key d940ce4b89c6375ba52a003f is also assigned under Norway (different country reading).
results.reviewer_notes: DROP applies only to this China-attributed candidate, not to the paper’s research quality or its valid Norway coverage.

results.verified_title: Artificial Intelligence and Foreign Information Manipulation: Chinese and Russian approaches
results.source_identity_basis: Opened the 32-page Hybrid CoE Paper 29 PDF, issued March 2026, and checked the cover/summary and Russia-specific substantive sections. The PDF heading identifies the exact assigned title and issuing organisation. The manifest’s 31 March date is a packaging approximation; publication itself is dated March 2026.
results.source_type: research institute policy analysis / threat-intelligence synthesis
results.evidence_location: PDF page 5 Summary; Russia-specific analysis pp. approximately 19–26; conclusions. Cross-check OpenAI 8 October 2026 observed Russian operation.
results.specific_finding: Russia-linked influence operators are using commercially available generative-AI tools to lower production costs and scale workflows, while indigenous frontier AI capabilities remain comparatively constrained; observed adoption is not proof of AI-technology leadership.
results.primary_evidence_summary: The Hybrid CoE synthesis finds AI-related manipulation activity since at least 2022, explains external tool dependence and the gap between Russia’s AI ambitions and capabilities, and describes varying Russia/China approaches. A later platform investigation independently documents a Russian false-front operation using AI for internal reports and synthetic influence materials.
results.corroboration_assessment: Independent OpenAI first-hand platform enforcement dated 8 October 2026 confirms concrete Russian AI-assisted workflows; EEAS 2026 threat reporting supports broader hybrid-threat context. Neither document measures Russian domestic model-training capacity, and EEAS cross-country aggregate figures must not be assigned solely to Russia.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: A distinctive asymmetric R&I pattern: operational adoption of externally available AI can advance despite frontier computing, model-development and hardware constraints. A technology-adoption / security capability finding, NOT proof Russia leads AI R&D.
results.eu_radar_comparison: Confirms the Radar’s documented divergence between Russian AI-enabled influence operations and technical-industrial AI capacity; refines claims about operational scale and validation.
results.method_and_limitations: Hybrid CoE blends case-study literature and documented incidents; evidence is incomplete and covert operations are selected for detection; outcome/reach estimates are not population-wide. OpenAI observes activity on its own platform, not total Russian ecosystem.
results.reviewer_notes: 2026-10-08 corroboration postdates the March report and is independently operationally grounded. Do not generalise all Chinese/Russian combined metrics to Russia.

results.verified_title: WIPO Global Innovation Index 2026 — United States indicators and innovation position
results.source_identity_basis: Opened WIPO’s official 2026 GII landing page and ranking; separately checked 2024/2025 WIPO editions. The matched item is WIPO’s indicator-based country assessment, not a US-government self-ranking. Independent US federal NCSES BERD 2024 survey released 29 October 2026 was also opened.
results.source_type: intergovernmental composite index plus independent national statistical survey
results.evidence_location: WIPO GII 2026 landing page, top-10 rank and country profile; WIPO GII 2024/2025 rank; NCSES BERD 2024 Table 1 and survey-description section.
results.specific_finding: The United States ranks 3rd in WIPO GII 2026 (also 3rd in 2024 and 2025), while its independently measured business R&D rose to US$765.1bn in 2024 (+6.0% from 2023). This supports a durable high-investment innovation system, not an improving overall GII rank.
results.primary_evidence_summary: WIPO 2026 lists Switzerland 1st, Sweden 2nd and USA 3rd. NCSES/Census BERD survey records $765.082bn US domestic business R&D in 2024 versus $721.792bn in 2023; own-funded share was about $679bn. Separate NCSES 2026 State of US S&E overview reports businesses performed 77% of estimated national R&D in 2024.
results.corroboration_assessment: NCSES is independent of WIPO and uses actual US enterprise-survey spending rather than composite country ranks; it corroborates the scale and business orientation, not WIPO’s ranking methodology. WIPO 2025 verifies that overall rank did not improve.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: Large commercial R&D investment and deep private-sector financing create industrial translation capacity; the GII composite captures multiple system pillars but cannot establish causation or single-technology superiority.
results.eu_radar_comparison: Not identified in the supplied main Radar. Adds independently measured innovation-system context, correcting any narrative that 2026 represents a US upward move in overall GII placement.
results.method_and_limitations: Composite rank sensitive to definitions, missing data and changing indicators; year-to-year ordinal rank is not causal. 2024 business R&D is historical data released October 2026, not 2026 R&D spending, and US dollars are nominal.
results.reviewer_notes: 2024 and 2025 WIPO rank also third. Do not mistake the 2024 reference year for a 2026 spending amount.

results.verified_title: UKRI backs quantum breakthroughs supported by training
results.source_identity_basis: Opened UKRI official article with published date 16 October 2026, project names and three separately quantified programme commitments; corroborating distinct UK government March 2026 quantum-policy announcement checked.
results.source_type: official grant and programme announcement, with independently published policy context
results.evidence_location: UKRI 16 October 2026: sections Supporting next generation systems; World-leading quantum sensing; Increasing quantum apprenticeship support. GOV.UK 17 March 2026 quantum package.
results.specific_finding: The UK announced a £50m commercial quantum-use project package, a separate £20m quantum-network capability programme and an £8m QuEST-apprenticeship expansion; these are 2026 public commitments, NOT independently demonstrated deployed capabilities.
results.primary_evidence_summary: UKRI names prospective application projects led by MoniRail (rail monitoring), Siloton (eye diagnostics) and ColdQuanta UK (mobile quantum radio); separate network component funding includes Aegiq. QuEST aims for 150 engineering apprentices by 2030. Earlier UK government programme announced up to £2bn quantum commitment.
results.corroboration_assessment: March UK quantum policy and October UK quantum-for-space technology roadmap independently show a longer-term national translation and skills strategy. They DO NOT independently audit UKRI award disbursements or field performance of the named products.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: Distinctive combined instrument mix targeting prototypes, domestic quantum-network supply chains and technical apprenticeships, moving R&I beyond foundational research toward industrial translation.
results.eu_radar_comparison: Not identified in main Radar: an actionable October 2026 UK industrial quantum and workforce commitment. Compare with EU quantum industrialisation only as parallel strategic approaches; do not presume completed UK advantage.
results.method_and_limitations: Official plans and award descriptions provide evidence of commitments but not product deployment, measured impact or completion of apprentice targets; budget categories must not be double-counted against headline national multi-year package.
results.reviewer_notes: The three stated components total £78m by simple arithmetic but may sit inside broader overlapping national strategies; avoid equating component sums with additional unique appropriation.

results.verified_title: FAPESP and NWO renew agreement and plan to expand scientific cooperation
results.source_identity_basis: Opened Agência FAPESP article dated 30 October 2026. It reports signatures on 26 October by São Paulo’s FAPESP and the Dutch Research Council NWO. Independently checked NWO board minutes of 24 May 2023 (released in bundled minutes PDF), which explicitly approved €1.5m for a Brazil–Netherlands bilateral initiative with FAPESP match, and NWO-hosted 2024 international call details for FAPESP.
results.source_type: institutional agreement report with independently documented bilateral-funding infrastructure
results.evidence_location: FAPESP article 30 October: first three paragraphs and Long-term partnership; NWO governing board minutes 24 May 2023, agenda h, allocation of €1.5m for Bilateraal Partnerschap Nederland–Brazilië; NWO DUT Call 2024 national annex pp. 61–62.
results.specific_finding: São Paulo’s FAPESP and the Netherlands’ NWO reported signing an extension on 26 October 2026 to maintain joint calls through 2028. The underlying bilateral co-funding mechanism is independently documented by NWO; planned international centres and a possible new 2028 memorandum are not yet executed.
results.primary_evidence_summary: The 2026 article describes signed amendment and multiple thematic expansions. NWO 2023 official minutes separately specify €1.5m reserved for a FAPESP–NWO bilateral partnership with partner matching commitment; its 2024 call lists separate FAPESP eligibility and research funding for São Paulo. The current amendment was not independently reproduced from the signed contract.
results.corroboration_assessment: Strong independent confirmation of a substantive historical FAPESP–NWO bilateral budget and a standing São Paulo international cofunding mechanism on nwo.nl. 2026 amendment date and terms are still asserted by one party and remain unaudited; independent NWO 2026 amendment text was not located.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: Subnational Brazilian research funder extends a functioning bilateral co-funding channel into future years, enabling internationally reviewed calls across energy, biodiversity, AI and health; relevant to Europe–Latin America science diplomacy and thematic funding interoperability.
results.eu_radar_comparison: Not identified in main Radar. Adds Brazil/São Paulo–Netherlands structural research-funding cooperation; potential research centres remain proposals, not achieved new institutions.
results.method_and_limitations: 2026 extension sourced to FAPESP self-report; NWO independent 2023/2024 records support the established funding mechanism, not the exact 2026 signed wording. São Paulo is not representative of all Brazilian federal research funding.
results.reviewer_notes: 2028 new memorandum explicitly planned, not signed. Some international research centres mentioned elsewhere in article are examples with other countries, not established Dutch/FAPESP centres. NWO board minutes are in Dutch; translated decision distinguishes budget reservation from completed grant disbursement.

results.verified_title: Capacity-building workshops are broadening participation in biodiversity research funding
results.source_identity_basis: Opened South African NRF article published 30 October 2026 under the assigned title and checked programme mechanism and second-call application statistics. The query-parameter form resolves the same official page after the unparameterised link failed in retrieval. South African government’s 3 September 2026 research-system speech independently describes national structural disparities.
results.source_type: institutional programme monitoring with independent system-level evidence
results.evidence_location: NRF article 30 October 2026: introduction, Responding to a participation gap, A regional approach to reach more researchers; official government NRF-awards speech 3 September 2026.
results.specific_finding: Historically disadvantaged institution (HDI) share of applications to the biodiversity FBIP second funding call rose from 3.7% in 2025 to 19.1% in 2026, while all applications increased 27→47 (+74.1%). This is a measurable one-year participation shift, not a proven long-term trend or funding-success effect.
results.primary_evidence_summary: NRF organised four regional proposal-development and awareness workshops with hybrid access, beginning late 2025 and involving 27 institutions initially. NRF’s own 2026 figures show expanded applications; decisions for some 2026 awards are pending. Independent government speech describes concentration of research funding and public measures to broaden access.
results.corroboration_assessment: Different government domain corroborates the existence and salience of research-participation inequity, not the exact FBIP application counts or causal effect of workshops. Treat 3.7% and 19.1% as first-party programme counts, unindependently audited.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: Targeted application-support workshops may lower institutional application barriers in a nationally unequal research-funding system. The finding is an early programme participation outcome and a testable inclusion mechanism.
results.eu_radar_comparison: Not identified in main Radar. Adds a measurable South African research-participation policy signal without claiming systemic funding equality has been achieved.
results.method_and_limitations: Small sample (27 to 47 total proposals), share shifts from a very low base, only two annual second-call observations and no comparison group; applications are not successful funding awards.
results.reviewer_notes: Two successive call cycles do not establish a multi-year trend. Do not infer workshop causality from correlational before/after counts.

results.verified_title: No One Builds Alone: The Geopolitics of AI Chips
results.source_identity_basis: The assigned DOI 10.38105/spr.vf5ks0gobi resolves to a 7 August 2026 MIT Science Policy Review item, an interview of chip-policy analyst Pranay Kotasthane by Zuzana Navratil; inspected publisher HTML and its PDF page(s), not an executed government programme report.
results.evidence_location: Science Policy Review interview opening and discussion of open design tools/process-development kits, pilot foundries and semiconductor talent; PDF introduction, title and interview format.
results.specific_finding: The interview argues that India needs greater access to chip-design knowledge, design-to-fab translation, shared infrastructure and international partnerships. It does NOT establish that the proposed open PDK or chip-pilot capability was deployed at national scale.
results.primary_evidence_summary: Pranay Kotasthane explains dependencies in advanced chip supply chains and proposes accessible design/fabrication approaches; no verified measurements of implementation, funding, yield or ecosystem adoption are offered as a new national result.
results.corroboration_assessment: EU–India Trade and Technology Council communication independently confirms policy interest in semiconductors and digital R&I collaboration, but not the specific interview’s suggested open-PDK/pilot-fab interventions.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: Relevant policy hypothesis for Indian semiconductor capability-building and global trusted-chain diversification; insufficient to classify as an achieved change, independently verified trend or distinctive implemented institution.
results.eu_radar_comparison: In main Radar. Changes characterization from possible realised R&I development to an interview-based recommendation needing programme-level evidence.
results.method_and_limitations: No field research methods, original experimental data or implementation evaluation; expert views may be persuasive but are not substantiation of realised government capacity.
results.reason_for_review_or_drop: Specific claimed structural improvement remains a proposal; independent evidence of operational shared PDKs/foundries and funded national rollout is missing.
results.reviewer_notes: The DOI and web article date may be represented differently in publisher URL path (July) and dated entry (August); source record date governs.

results.verified_title: Between Weltoffenheit and securitisation: Germany’s partial securitisation of science policy towards the People’s Republic of China
results.source_identity_basis: Verified exact DOI/title in European Politics and Society publisher index and substantive abstract/section descriptions; dated 2 September 2026. Direct Taylor & Francis page blocked by 403. The article explicitly analyses German discourses and science-policy institutionalisation concerning China.
results.source_type: academic interpretive study of German science policy
results.evidence_location: Publisher indexed abstract, introduction and conclusion: German policy phases and research-security discourse toward China, 2014–2026.
results.specific_finding: The work documents Germany’s partial securitisation of scientific collaboration WITH China; China is a perceived external partner/risk in German policy discourse, not the policy actor under empirical study.
results.primary_evidence_summary: Historical/interpretive examination of Germany’s open-science (“Weltoffenheit”) versus securitisation stance and selectively institutionalised safeguards. The paper states that it does not systematically reconstruct Chinese policies.
results.corroboration_assessment: Independent Scandinavian comparison also concerns European responses to China, so does not establish China-side R&I institutional changes. Do not count an unrelated Chinese statistical bulletin as corroboration of this paper’s German policy mechanism.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: Valid German/European research-security development, but out-of-scope under the assigned China domestic research-institutions regional question.
results.eu_radar_comparison: Main Radar contains the exact paper: change country assignment or add German/EU context; no reason to purge the legitimate paper from the Radar on this basis alone.
results.method_and_limitations: Main paper full HTML fetch blocked. Available publisher substantive abstract/index sufficiently resolves geographic subject; interpretive framing does not causally measure changes in Chinese R&I institutions.
results.reason_for_review_or_drop: Misassigned to China as a national R&I change; study explicitly centres Germany’s policy. Regional mismatch is substantive, not a source-quality complaint.
results.reviewer_notes: Cross-border topic labels should distinguish “country discussed” from “country whose institutions were actually studied.”

results.verified_title: Digital architecture of information governance for education and research in Ukraine
results.source_identity_basis: Assigned DOI 10.46299/j.isjea.20260504.07 matched the International Science Journal of Engineering & Agriculture publisher article by Anastasiya Ilyina, publication 1 August 2026 and pp. 81–94. Opened article metadata/full descriptive sections; it discusses proposed framework rather than a deployed government system.
results.source_type: single-author conceptual policy architecture / analytical synthesis
results.evidence_location: Publisher article abstract, proposed digital-architecture model and data–analytics–decisions–outcomes sequence; concluding implementation discussion.
results.specific_finding: The paper proposes integrated information governance for Ukrainian education and research and asserts fragmentation of data/reporting; no independently demonstrated deployment or measured increase in state R&I performance has been verified.
results.primary_evidence_summary: The author diagnoses siloed data/reporting and formulates a layered digital-governance model. Proposed integration is an analytical recommendation, not a proven reform, operating interoperable platform or independently replicated data-quality finding.
results.corroboration_assessment: European Commission sources corroborate separate ongoing Ukrainian R&I-system and research-infrastructure reconstruction, including repository initiatives, but do not verify that the specific proposed governance architecture was implemented or independently measure its claimed systemic fragmentation.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: A potentially useful framework for rebuilding evidence-based research administration, open data interoperability and evaluation systems during wartime reconstruction; actionable only if tied to actual implementing institutions and measurable system outcomes.
results.eu_radar_comparison: Exact work in main Radar: refine from implied accomplished digital system to proposed architecture and diagnosed challenges; empirical status remains unresolved.
results.method_and_limitations: Conceptual model; no controlled rollout, user adoption data, causal impact estimates or observed cross-system interoperability in this paper. Article’s diagnosis should not be re-labelled as an achieved reform.
results.reason_for_review_or_drop: Independent operational evidence for the model and representative measurement of national data fragmentation is missing.
results.reviewer_notes: DOI and publisher URL identities established despite publisher article view differing from DOI resolution URL.

results.verified_title: Global Fusion Energy Trends — Report from the F4E Fusion Observatory: Funding, Performance, Research and Innovation
results.source_identity_basis: The exact assigned 15 July 2026 Fusion for Energy report is linked from the publisher’s opened official companion announcement, and its title/date/subject match; however the 14 MB assigned PDF repeatedly failed direct source opening, so underlying report methodology, figures and annexes were not inspected fully.
results.source_type: intergovernmental research-technology comparative report; original full PDF inaccessible in this scan
results.evidence_location: Publisher substantive report announcement 15 July 2026 (overview of US/EU/China comparisons, categories funding and patents); original PDF pages/tables not independently inspected.
results.specific_finding: Publisher’s accessible summary reports a strong US private-fusion-capital position alongside China’s larger patent share and Europe’s publication/ITER strengths; do not treat summary figures as fully verified until full methodological tables are checked.
results.primary_evidence_summary: F4E’s publisher article gives around €7.38bn in identified US fusion funding and €2.41bn US private capital versus €6.94bn identified for China and €3.34bn for the EU (source-defined windows/currency). It also indicates differences in patent-family distribution and no presently power-plant-level plasma performance. Exact comparability across categories is not verified without reading the full PDF.
results.corroboration_assessment: Publisher companion gives substantive content but is NOT independent corroboration. Fusion Industry Association independently confirms significant commercial fusion fundraising (global survey), but its time frame and definitions differ and cannot directly validate F4E’s regional totals. The 14 MB original PDF could not be opened for methods.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: Plausible distinctive US commercial-fusion capital strength, with value for comparative industrial maturation, commercialization and supply-chain analysis; no proof of technological readiness based solely on financing.
results.eu_radar_comparison: Exact main Radar entry exists. Tentatively supports differentiated EU/US/China strengths, but do not promote to verified finding until complete report and definitions are checked.
results.method_and_limitations: Critical limitation: assigned report full PDF inaccessible due file-size/fetch errors. Industry survey covers a different population, period, currency and measurement basis. Patents, spending and technical readiness are noninterchangeable metrics.
results.reason_for_review_or_drop: Substantive assigned source was not actually opened; fails mandatory full/substantive-section evidence check against original report, so REVIEW despite plausible corroborated industry context.
results.reviewer_notes: Publisher article was opened and read; no invented page citations to inaccessible original PDF. Do not use industry $14.24bn total as if comparable to F4E € figures.

results.verified_title: Governing the de-risking agenda: policy instrument mixes in Scandinavian research collaboration with China — Norway case
results.source_identity_basis: The assigned DOI, title and online publication date 28 March 2026 match publisher-indexed full sections and Lund University research record. Checked Norway-specific Results §5.2, Method §4 and concluding comparative analysis, alongside Norwegian government directorate’s independently opened study of researcher experiences.
results.source_type: academic comparative research-policy study with qualitative empirical inputs
results.evidence_location: Full publisher-indexed content: §§4.1–4.2 methods; §5.2 Norway (enabling instruments, replacement, reinforcement, layering); §6 Discussion; §7 Conclusions.
results.specific_finding: Norway has a layered/negotiated research-security governance model balancing cooperation with China and risk mitigation. National guidelines, a China Round Table and specialised export-licensing body DEKSA coexist rather than imposing a single university rulebook.
results.primary_evidence_summary: Norway issued responsible international-collaboration guidelines in 2023; established DEKSA export-licensing administration in 2025 and uses the China Round Table to interpret policy with universities and other stakeholders. The round table does not impose a unified position; local HEI decisions vary. The research expressly cautions against attributing causal policy outcomes to instrument mixes.
results.corroboration_assessment: Norwegian Directorate for Higher Education and Skills independently documents qualitative researcher/institutional experiences under geopolitical tensions and provides operational guidance on export control and responsible cooperation. This corroborates actual national institutional practice, not numerical effectiveness.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: A meaningful non-EU European research-security governance difference: negotiated, sector-linked steering can preserve academic flexibility yet create local uncertainty and unequal burden. Relevant comparator for EU member states designing China-related research safeguards.
results.eu_radar_comparison: Confirms and extends the main Radar interpretation with named Norwegian operational mechanisms and independent national institution evidence; the same DOI also appears under China but should not be treated as Chinese domestic R&I policy.
results.method_and_limitations: Comparative policy-instrument analysis using documents and stakeholder interviews is illustrative, not causally identified; only three Scandinavian countries studied, and expert responses may not capture all HEIs. Some official documents are implementation guidance rather than audited outcomes.
results.reviewer_notes: Duplicate document key with China item is a region-tag issue, not duplicate country finding. Publisher HTML direct fetch returned 403 but substantial full-text indexed source and university repository were examined.

results.verified_title: The Fourth Dimension of Science Diplomacy
results.source_identity_basis: Assigned DOI/title located through NIScPR Science Diplomacy issue listing and repository record: Victor M. Castaño and Galileo Violini, Volume 10 Issue 1 (July–September 2026), pages 3–6. The manifest date 2026-01-01 does not match the journal issue. Publisher article full text was not retrievable in this scan.
results.evidence_location: Science Diplomacy Volume 10 Issue 1 table of contents and NIScPR repository metadata, pages 3–6; manifest extract discusses global geopolitical tensions and science diplomacy.
results.specific_finding: The article describes an international science-diplomacy conceptual framework and research-security debate, not a documented change in Mexican science funding, institutions or international-agreement practice.
results.primary_evidence_summary: Conceptual argument on new dimensions of science diplomacy; the authors’ locations or affiliations do not establish Mexico as the country researched. No Mexican policy instrument, dated national event, budget or observed outcome was established.
results.corroboration_assessment: Independent substantive Mexico-specific corroboration was not found. Both links help establish publisher/issue identity, not a national Mexico R&I finding. The full article could not be inspected; conservative DROP is based on available topic and country mismatch.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: Science-diplomacy theory can inform worldwide discussions but is not a Mexico-specific, independently evidenced R&I change.
results.eu_radar_comparison: No matching entry identified in main Radar; dropping this discovered candidate does not alter any Radar coverage.
results.method_and_limitations: Publisher issue metadata and provided excerpt suggest a general commentary, not longitudinal empirical research or a Mexico case. Full article inaccessible, limiting assessment of any additional examples; date recorded only as issue quarter.
results.reason_for_review_or_drop: Country inference appears to have come from author affiliation, not article subject. Manifest 2026-01-01 bibliographic date inconsistent with Volume 10(1) July–September 2026.
results.reviewer_notes: If later full text unexpectedly reveals an analysed Mexican case, re-open as REVIEW with that explicit passage; do not infer national attribution from metadata.
